clue.text: Deserved relaxation eventually, being lugged around

indicators.note: around says the eared letters are wrapped about the single letter from relaxation

parts.note: lugs are ears, so something lugged is eared, having ears

indicators.note: eventually points to what comes at the very end of the word relaxation

parts.note: its final letter

explanation.surface: Someone who has been hauled about all day has earned a rest at last.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lugged' looks like carried, but lugs are ears in British slang, so 'being lugged' is EARED; it goes around N, the end of 'relaxation'.
explanation.definitionFit: To have earned something is to have deserved it through effort or merit, a straight synonym.

clue.text: Money maker a failure? Not entirely

indicators.note: not entirely means the word is cut short, losing its last letter

parts.note: a miss is a failure to hit

explanation.surface: Someone wonders whether a moneymaking scheme was a flop.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Money maker' is not a mint but Martin Amis, who wrote the novel Money.
explanation.definitionFit: The British novelist Martin Amis is the author of the 1984 novel Money, so he made it.

clue.text: It is essential, born on earth, to accept some failing occasionally

parts.note: née marks a woman's maiden name, meaning born

indicators.note: to accept means the dust takes in the letters picked from some

parts.note: dust is earth or soil, as in dust to dust

indicators.note: only now and then do the letters of some survive, the others failing

parts.note: its first and third letters

explanation.surface: A grim maxim that essential life on earth involves the odd failure.
explanation.walkthrough: 'On' in a down clue puts the first piece above the next.
explanation.definitionFit: The saying 'needs must when the devil drives' means one must do what is necessary, so it is essential.

clue.text: Modern business caught up in catastrophe

indicators.note: in places the turned letters inside the word for catastrophe

parts.note: doom is ruin or disaster

indicators.note: up in a down clue tells us the two letters read from bottom to top

parts.note: ct is a cricket scorer's abbreviation for caught

explanation.surface: A modern firm gets dragged into a disaster.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface recalls dotcom firms caught up in the 2000 bust, a nod to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A dotcom is a company trading on the internet, a newer kind of enterprise.

clue.text: Bag is in right end of busy dressing room

parts.note: a sac is a bag-like pouch

indicators.note: in says the word is goes inside the abbreviation for right

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: end of picks the last letter of busy

parts.note: its final letter

explanation.surface: Someone describes stuffing a bag into the corner of a crowded changing area.
explanation.walkthrough: RT is the less common abbreviation for right, needed here so that IS can sit inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: A sacristy is the room in a church where clergy put on their vestments, a dressing room for services.

clue.text: Breaded fish women organised after children's game and before church

indicators.note: after places the women's letters following the game and the word and
before puts those letters ahead of the church abbreviation

parts.note: sardines is a hide-and-seek game where seekers squeeze into the hider's spot
WI is the Women's Institute, a British organisation of women

explanation.surface: A recipe for crumbed fish, with women's groups busy around a party game and a church service.
explanation.walkthrough: The Women's Institute (WI) is a British community group for women.
explanation.definitionFit: A sandwich puts fish between slices of bread, so its sardines are in a jocular sense breaded.

clue.text: Monument not cheap to sculpt

indicators.note: sculpting reshapes material, so the letters are reshaped

explanation.surface: A memorial is costly to carve.
explanation.definitionFit: A cenotaph is a memorial to the dead buried elsewhere, like London's war memorial in Whitehall.

clue.text: A lot of lies not initially a problem

indicators.note: not initially says the first letter is removed

parts.note: a tissue of lies is a mass of lies

explanation.surface: A web of untruths is not at first a problem.
explanation.walkthrough: The idiom 'a tissue of lies' gives the word to trim.
explanation.definitionFit: An issue is a matter of concern, a difficulty to resolve.

clue.text: Indulgence of endlessly pilfered allowance

indicators.note: endlessly shaves off the letters at both ends of the word

parts.note: pilfered means stolen
a ration is a fixed allowance

explanation.surface: Someone forgiving takes a lenient view of a pinched share.
explanation.definitionFit: Toleration is forbearance, putting up with something, which is indulgence in the lenient sense.

clue.text: Really excellent ball game cheers king

parts.note: fives is a British game in which a ball is struck against walls with the hand
ta is British informal thanks, like cheers
R, from Latin rex, is the usual abbreviation for king

explanation.surface: A fan raves about a match, toasting the monarch.
explanation.walkthrough: Fives is a British handball-like court game; ta is British slang for thanks, which is what 'cheers' also means.
explanation.definitionFit: A five-star rating marks the top grade in hotel or review scales, hence outstanding quality.

clue.text: Food manufacturers are in protected position

definitions.meaning: first meaning: the big Swiss multinational behind KitKat and Nescafé
second meaning: to lie snugly in a sheltered spot

explanation.walkthrough: The company name and the verb are spelt alike apart from the accent; the plural verb 'are' fits a company treated as many people.
explanation.definitionFit: Nestlé is a multinational foods company, and to nestle is to settle cosily somewhere sheltered.

clue.text: Vaccination booster?

parts.note: a figurative phrase for something that revives or encourages, read literally as an injection

explanation.walkthrough: A booster jab literally is an injection into the arm; the idiom means a fillip that lifts spirits or fortunes.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means an encouraging lift, and taken literally it describes being injected with a vaccine.

clue.text: In a row preserving alliance is concerning high-ranking politician

indicators.note: preserving keeps the alliance safe within the word for in a row

parts.note: serial describes things coming one after another, in a row
NATO is the North Atlantic Treaty Organisation, a military alliance

explanation.surface: A quarrel threatens an alliance involving a top statesman.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Row' tempts one to read argument; here it is a line, giving serial.
explanation.definitionFit: Senatorial is an adjective meaning relating to a senator, a member of a legislature's upper house.

clue.text: Live with a socially superior admirer

parts.note: to be is to exist or live
U means upper-class, from Nancy Mitford's U and non-U usage

explanation.surface: Advice to a social climber to move in with an upper-class suitor.
explanation.walkthrough: U for upper-class comes from the 1950s British 'U and non-U' debate on posh speech.
explanation.definitionFit: A beau is a boyfriend or male suitor, someone who admires and courts another.

clue.text: Sacked, one inept dancer who is so unnaturally tall?

definitions.text: dancer who is so unnaturally tall?

indicators.note: sacked, like a ransacked town, means turned over and pillaged, so the letters are thrown about

explanation.surface: An incompetent ballet dancer is fired.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sacked' reads as dismissed, which suits 'one inept', but it signals the rearrangement.
explanation.definitionFit: A ballerina on the tips of her toes stands higher than her natural height, the position named by this French phrase.

clue.text: Become part of group felling giant tree

indicators.note: felling knocks the tree down, collapsing its letters into disorder

explanation.surface: Lumberjacks join a team to bring down a huge tree.
explanation.definitionFit: To integrate is to join and blend into a community or group as a full member.

clue.text: Emphasise bell stops contest

indicators.note: stops as in plugs a gap, the bell sitting inside the contest

parts.note: a bout is a fight or contest
to ring is the sound a bell makes

explanation.surface: At a boxing match, the bell halts the round.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stops' looks like the bell ending the bout, but it means plugs, putting RING inside.
explanation.definitionFit: To bring out a quality is to highlight or accentuate it, making it stand out.

clue.text: Police chief overrides law for possibly harmful agents

indicators.note: overrides is read as rides over, the chief's name straddling the law on both sides

parts.note: Lavrentiy Beria headed Stalin's secret police
an act is a law passed by parliament

explanation.surface: A senior officer ignores the law in pursuit of dangerous agents.
explanation.walkthrough: The police chief is not a generic title but Beria, head of the Soviet NKVD.
explanation.definitionFit: Some bacteria cause disease, so they are microbes that may do harm, hence 'possibly'.

clue.text: Astroturf is too much for left-winger

indicators.note: the longer word holds more than enough letters, so the answer sits inside it

parts.note: the letters run on in the middle of this word

explanation.surface: Someone complains that playing on an artificial pitch is unbearable for a winger on the left.
explanation.walkthrough: The left-winger is not a footballer but a Trotskyist; a trot is British slang for one.
explanation.definitionFit: A Trot is informal shorthand for a Trotskyist, someone on the far left of politics.

clue.text: Simple restaurant's gravy overcomes resistance

indicators.note: overcomes in a down clue: the gravy brand comes over and around the resistance

parts.note: Bisto is a well-known British brand of gravy powder
R is the symbol for electrical resistance

explanation.surface: A cheap café's gravy wins over a sceptical diner.
explanation.walkthrough: Bisto is a British gravy granule brand; the 's of 'restaurant's' is just 'has'.
explanation.definitionFit: A bistro is a small, informal eatery serving modest food.

clue.text: Love acting, without hope of success

parts.note: love is a score of nothing in tennis
acting means doing something

explanation.surface: A would-be performer whose stage career is going nowhere.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is an informal refusal or verdict that there is no chance, as when a plan is hopeless.

clue.text: Captain Ahab for one losing weight gets fitter

indicators.note: losing means the weight letter goes

parts.note: Ahab in Moby-Dick captains a whaling ship, so he is a whaler

explanation.surface: Moby-Dick's captain sheds pounds and gets in shape.
explanation.definitionFit: Hale means healthy, so haler is the comparative, in better health.

clue.text: Capital both sides lost in trade union's protest

indicators.note: both sides lost removes the outer letters at either end

parts.note: a go-slow is industrial action by working deliberately slowly

explanation.surface: A city strike where both factions lose out.
explanation.definitionFit: Oslo is the capital city of Norway.

clue.text: Boiler given oxygen going vigorously like this?

parts.note: a billy is a camping can for boiling water
O is the chemical symbol for oxygen

explanation.surface: A boiler fed with extra oxygen roars away.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Like billy-o' is a British idiom for 'with great energy'; the definition asks for the word completing that phrase.
explanation.definitionFit: Doing something like billy-o means doing it furiously or with gusto, so the word stands for that vigour.

clue.text: His toast wants a spread? I don't believe you

indicators.note: spreading the letters about scatters them into a new order, as butter is spread

explanation.surface: Someone claims their toast needs butter, and a listener scoffs.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase voices doubt or scepticism at a claim, just as saying you don't believe someone does.

clue.text: Uncanny children almost messing with time

indicators.note: messing with suggests muddling the letters together
almost drops the final letter of the word children

parts.note: the word minus its last letter
T is the physics abbreviation for time

explanation.surface: Kids fooling about with a clock.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Almost' trims CHILDREN to CHILDRE; 'messing with' then shuffles CHILDRE plus T.
explanation.definitionFit: Eldritch is a Scottish-origin literary word for weird, eerie or unearthly.

clue.text: Old district, not one part of America

indicators.note: not says the numeral for one is left out of the word for district

parts.note: a region is a district or area
I is the Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: A former area is said to be no longer one unit.
explanation.definitionFit: Oregon is a state in the Pacific Northwest of the United States.
